papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: Vibrotactile stimulation on the upper back requires stronger vibration during goal-directed reaching but does not impede reaching performance
papers.abstract: Vibrotactile stimulation is a promising method of biofeedback, with potential applications for ergonomic posture and balance, rehabilitation, and motor learning. These applications require balancing tactile perception with motor performance and cognitive workload. In this study, participants performed a detection task, a reaching task, and a concurrent reach-and-detect task, with vibrotactile signals delivered on the hand or upper back. Sensitivity to stimuli, motor performance, and cognitive workload were compared for each task. Sensitivity was suppressed during movement, but this suppression was greater on hand compared to the upper back. Movement time was slowed by vibration on the hand but not the upper back. Mental workload and task complexity increased for the reach-and-detect task compared to the individual tasks. We conclude that vibrotactile feedback devices worn on the upper back do not impede motor performance, with only minor tactile suppression. This could be overcome by presenting highly salient or personalized feedback.

papers.title: Functional characterization of the 26RFa/orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamic area reveals their key role in the control of glucose homeostasis
papers.abstract: Defining the nature and molecular mechanisms of the neurocircuitry controlling glucose homeostasis is crucial in understanding how alterations in these pathways promote the development of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here, we functionally characterize a population of lateral hypothalamic neurons co-expressing the anti-hyperglycemic neuropeptides 26RFa and orexin. Using complementary chemogenetic, pharmacological and genetic approaches, including mice deficient for 26RFa, orexin or both neuropeptides, we investigated the respective contribution of each signaling system to glucose homeostasis. We found that lateral hypothalamic 26RFa neurons extensively co-express orexin, defining a distinct peptidergic population with convergent anti-hyperglycemic properties. Unexpectedly, chemogenetic activation of these neurons potentiated glucose-induced hyperglycemia despite the anti-hyperglycemic properties of both neuropeptides. To understand this paradox, we examined the transcriptional responses of the 26RFa and orexin peptidergic systems and found that neuronal activation was associated with coordinated, glycemic state-dependent downregulation of both signaling systems. Furthermore, genetic loss-of-function approaches revealed distinct contributions of the two neuropeptidergic systems, with orexin signaling mediating most of the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation, whereas 26RFa signaling is required for the dynamic regulation of orexin expression. Finally, our findings provide new insights into the functional organization of lateral hypothalamic 26RFa/orexin neurons and advance our understanding of how coordinated neuropeptidergic signaling contributes to systemic glucose homeostasis.

papers.title: Diurnal Variations in the Cholinergic System of the Nucleus Accumbens
papers.abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) plays a critical role in reward-related behaviors, which exhibit diurnal variations. Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are the primary source of acetylcholine within the NAc and regulate local dopamine (DA) signaling through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Although there are diurnal variations in NAc dynamics, little is known about whether CIN activity and nicotinic signaling also vary across the light/dark cycle. Here, we aimed to determine diurnal variations in the NAc cholinergic system using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and cell-attached electrophysiological recordings in male rodents. We examined time-of-day-dependent differences in nAChR-mediated modulation of DA release, spontaneous CIN firing frequency, and firing patterns. We found that spontaneous CIN firing varied across the light/dark cycle, with increased activity during the dark cycle. Additionally, bath application of nicotine (NIC), mecamylamine (MEC), and dihydro-{beta}-erythroidine (DH{beta}E) reduced CIN firing frequency during the dark cycle, with only MEC decreasing firing frequency in the light cycle. NIC and MEC also altered CIN firing patterns during the dark cycle, whereas DH{beta}E primarily affected firing frequency. Together, these findings demonstrate diurnal variations in NAc CIN activity and reveal time-of-day-dependent differences in the effects of nAChR modulation on spontaneous firing. These results suggest that nicotinic signaling may contribute to diurnal regulation of NAc cholinergic activity, providing insight into mechanisms underlying time-of-day-dependent changes in reward circuitry.

papers.title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
papers.abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

papers.title: Temporal tuning of actin nucleation by the repurposed DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 encodes distinct axon guidance decisions
papers.abstract: Axon guidance is essential for neural circuit assembly and function. While much of the repertoire of guidance cues and receptors is known, its limited diversity cannot fully explain the remarkable complexity of the brain connectome. How temporally ordered, context-dependent intrinsic programs shape the diversity of axonal responses to guidance signals remains poorly understood. We reveal how non-canonical Wnt5a signalling repurposes the DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 as a downstream integrator to control retinal ganglion cell axon decision-making at the midline. We demonstrate that differential RAD51/fignl1 expression and interaction dynamics between ipsilateral and contralateral axons tunes the magnitude and temporal dynamics of F-actin nucleation, thereby encoding their trajectory choice. Our findings establish temporal control of cytoskeletal dynamics as a key determinant of axon decision-making and thereby a fundamental layer of circuit wiring. They provide a potential mechanistic framework linking mutations in the DNA repair gene RAD51 to neurodevelopmental disorders with midline guidance defects.

papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

papers.title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

papers.title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
papers.abstract: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

papers.title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
papers.abstract: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

papers.title: Exposure to childhood adversity and adult alcohol, nicotine, and illicit drug use in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO)
papers.abstract: Rationale: Exposure to adversity in childhood and adolescence (i.e., "early-life stress"; ELS) is a well-established risk factor for substance use. Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate associations between ELS exposure and substance use across subtypes of ELS, different substance classes, and behavioral profiles of substance use. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined associations between ELS exposure and substance use in a population-based sample of 172,173 adults aged 19-74 years from the German National Cohort (NAKO). ELS exposure was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Screener. Substance use included nicotine, alcohol, and illicit drug use. Associations were examined using regression models evaluating overall ELS exposure, cumulative trauma load, and ELS subtypes. Latent class analysis (LCA) was conducted to identify substance use profiles. Results: ELS exposure was associated with higher odds of smoking, greater smoking severity, heavier alcohol consumption among drinkers, and higher odds of lifetime illicit drug use. Overall, the strongest associations were observed for opioid and stimulant use. Dose-response analyses revealed higher risk with increasing numbers of ELS subtypes. Abuse-related subtypes, particularly exposure to physical and sexual abuse, consistently showed strongest independent associations across substances, whereas neglect exhibited weaker, more variable associations. LCA identified four substance use profiles, with ELS exposure predicting membership in more severe polysubstance classes. Conclusions: ELS emerged as a robust risk factor for adult substance use, underscoring the need for trauma-informed approaches in clinical practice, public health, and policy to mitigate the long-term consequences of early adversity.

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

papers.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
papers.abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

papers.title: Pilifers provide rapid mechanosensory feedback during floral tracking in hawkmoths
papers.abstract: Hawkmoths expertly hover over flowers during feeding, accurately tracking floral movements even as flowers gently sway in the wind. They use visual and mechanosensory feedback to adjust their position, while their long, flexible mouthpart, the proboscis, stays inserted inside the nectar spur. Although much is known about how hawkmoths detect and process visual motion, far less is understood about how hawkmoths detect mechanical motion cues. Pilifers are hair bundles at the proboscis-head joint, well-positioned to provide feedback about floral motion. Here, we tested if pilifers could provide mechanosensory feedback essential for successful floral tracking. We computed bending at the proboscis base during floral tracking in freely flying hawkmoths and found that floral movements induce small yet significantly correlated lateral bending. Recordings from pilifer afferents showed that they respond to lateral motions of amplitudes similar to those seen in natural floral tracking behaviors. They respond to different directions and speeds of proboscis motion with an average latency of 1.9 ms. Neural tracing revealed extensive sensory arborizations in the sub-esophageal ganglion of the brain and ventral nerve cord, indicating a feedback pathway to the neck and flight motor system that enables rapid coordination of appendages and body for successful feeding.

papers.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human. Keywords: Speech neuroprosthesis, paralinguistics, BCI, naturalistic communication

papers.title: Action-related brain dynamics during leader-follower coordination
papers.abstract: Leader-follower dynamics are essential for social interaction, enabling smooth inter-personal coordination. Although neuroimaging studies have identified brain networks associated with leading and following, the dynamical brain signatures supporting these roles remain poorly characterized. Here, sixteen dyads performed a joint-improvisation mirror-game task with predefined leader-follower roles while magnetoencephalography (MEG) and hand kinematics (acceleration) were simultaneously recorded. We investigated role-specific modulations of source-space MEG activity in delta (0.54 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (40-90 Hz) frequency bands, as well as coherence between cortical activity and movement kinematics. Compared with leaders, followers exhibited stronger theta-band activity in a cluster comprising frontal, cingulate, and sensorimotor regions, and stronger coherence between movement kinematics and occipital cortical activity, consistent with enhanced monitoring, adaptation, and reliance on visual kinematic information. In contrast, leaders showed reduced alpha-band power in sensorimotor and premotor regions, and stronger beta-band activity in occipital cortices, likely reflecting greater demands for action planning and predictive control. Our results identify complementary spectral and action-related brain signatures associated with leader-follower coordination during joint improvisation, providing new insights into the neural underpinnings of real-time interpersonal coordination.

papers.title: An anatomy-constrained transcriptomic screen identifies a 19-gene panel with an ordered regional similarity pattern in the human somatosensory system
papers.abstract: Neuroanatomical pathways link specialized brain regions, but whether regional transcriptomic profiles preserve relationships aligned with pathway order remains unclear. We defined candidate pathways and their available tissue representations from neuroanatomical literature, then screened 10,262 genes in the Body Index of Gene Expression (BIGE), a human microarray resource covering cells and tissues. The screen required expression across every mapped region of a route and limited single-region dominance. It identified 23 candidates in three routes with sufficient coverage; 19 met the criteria for the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) representation and formed the fixed panel. We evaluated this panel in six Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) donors across three central regional representations: an aggregate of samples assigned to the cuneate and gracile nuclei (Cu/Gr), the lateral group of nuclei, ventral division, within the dorsal thalamus (DTLv), and postcentral gyrus. The regional-order contrast compared the mean similarity of the pairs adjacent in the anatomical sequence, Cu/Gr-DTLv and DTLv-postcentral gyrus, with Cu/Gr-postcentral gyrus similarity. Both adjacent-in-order correlations were positive in all six donors; the contrast was positive in five and reached a mean of T = 0.345175 (exact sign test, P = 0.109375). The panel exceeded two distributions of 50,000 gene sets generated under comparable selection constraints (P = 0.027919 and P = 0.026579). In descriptive anatomical comparisons, it ranked third among 240 combinations and first among the target and all 16 single-region substitutions. All 50,000 one-probe-per-gene analyses retained T > 0, and broad neuronal-expression contrasts were positive in medulla, thalamus, and cortex. Spatial support depended on the null model, with stronger evidence under whole-donor surrogates (P = 0.003860) than under the primary within-compartment model (P = 0.051179). These findings identify a fixed gene panel whose regional similarity is aligned with the represented central order of the DCML system and define a specific hypothesis for prospective evaluation in an independent, anatomically resolved dataset.

papers.title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
papers.abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Longitudinal associations between task-control network functioning, cognition, and the environment in early adolescence
papers.abstract: Neural maturation in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks is thought to support the development of adolescents' cognitive and adaptive functioning. Further, theory suggests that family and neighborhood contexts shape brain network development. Yet, few longitudinal studies have examined the co-development of brain network mechanisms with cognitive and adaptive functioning or with environmental factors that could shape the maturation of these mechanisms. The present study addressed these gaps. We used longitudinal data spanning late childhood (Mage=10 years) to early adolescence (Mage=12) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (n=4862). Stable and construct-valid neural signatures of task-control network functioning were estimated using longitudinal bifactor modeling of neural responses to cognitive demand during the n-back task. Multivariate latent change-score models were used to examine co-development of this signature with cognitive efficiency (drift rate from the diffusion model), teacher-reported attention problems, family conflict, and neighborhood safety. Models accounted for baseline family income. Robust reciprocal relations between task-control activation and cognitive efficiency were identified and the latent change scores for efficiency and task-control activation were positively correlated. Similar reciprocal associations were observed between cognitive efficiency and attention problems. Baseline family income predicted the rate of change in task-control network functioning. This study demonstrates that task-control network functioning co-develops with cognition, which in turn supports attentional functioning development across early adolescence. Further, findings highlight the utility of this neural signature of task-control network functioning for understanding the neural basis of cognitive development and the mechanisms through which environmental experiences shape brain and behavior.

papers.title: Fast Generalized Longitudinal Functional Principal Components Analysis with Applications to Population-Level Neuronal Dynamics
papers.abstract: Functional data are widely collected across many fields. One approach for modeling functional data collected across repeated measures is longitudinal functional PCA (LFPCA), which allows for the decomposition of variability at multiple levels. However, existing estimation approaches for LFPCA can be computationally demanding for large or high-dimensional datasets. Here, we propose fast generalized LFPCA, a novel estimation technique that bins data along the functional domain and fits a marginal mixed model at each bin. Simulation results show that the proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques while achieving similar accuracy, making LFPCA scalable to datasets with more densely sampled observations and larger sample sizes. We apply the proposed technique to model neuronal firing rate data both on and off deep brain stimulation (DBS) to investigate how the intervention modulates population-level neuronal activity. Our results suggest that the vast majority of between-neuron variation can be explained by four principal components, which relate to individual differences in neuronal firing as well as the arm manipulation paradigm under study. We also find that DBS significantly increases the variability of firing activity, likely driven by increased firing from a subset of neurons in response to DBS, a novel insight not obtained in previous analyses. Code to implement the proposed method and run simulation studies is included in the supplement.

papers.title: Perineuronal nets in the bed nucleus of stria terminalis mediate stress-induced anxiety behaviour in adult male mice
papers.abstract: Anxiety disorders affect an estimated 301.4 million people globally. However, they remain among the most challenging conditions to treat, with only around half of patients reporting a 50% or greater reduction in their symptoms. The discovery of novel and more effective treatments therefore requires a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of anxiety at both the circuit and cellular levels. Stress induces aberrant changes in neuronal plasticity across brain regions within the anxiety circuitry including the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). One mechanism through which synaptic plasticity is regulated is the organisation of perineuronal nets (PNNs), specialised extracellular matrix structures that are highly sensitive to stress. In rodent models, stress is associated with a reduction in PNN number and/or decreased Wisteria floribunda Agglutinin (WFA) labelling in limbic areas. However, the development of PNNs within the BNST and their role in the stress responsiveness remain largely unknown. In the current study we investigated the spatiotemporal development of PNNs within the BNST of male mice, where they first appear at P30 and continue to mature into adulthood, reaching their highest expression at P210 and specifically within the anteromedial BNST. We further showed that stress-induced anxiety is associated with a reduction in PNN number and significant changes to PNN fine structure including increased leakiness in the anteromedial BNST. Most importantly, enzymatic removal of PNNs by chondroitinase ABC in the mouse anteromedial BNST exacerbated behavioural responses to acute stress as demonstrated by increased anxiety-like behaviour. Collectively, these results highlight an indispensable role for PNNs within the anteromedial BNST in mediating a healthy emotional response to psychosocial stress.

papers.title: NeuroMark dFNC: Transferable Dynamic-State Templates for Subject-Specific and Frequency-Resolved Chronnectomics
papers.abstract: Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) commonly identifies recurring connectivity states from resting-state fMRI, but states derived independently in each dataset lack guaranteed correspondence across studies and cannot be directly estimated in new participants. We introduce NeuroMark dFNC, which extends the NeuroMark principle of prior-guided network estimation to dynamic connectivity by using reproducible reference states as priors for estimating corresponding subject-specific states. Reference-state templates were derived from UK Biobank using windowed functional network connectivity and time-frequency moments (TFMs), with split-sample reproducibility evaluated for k-means, independent component analysis (ICA), and principal component analysis (PCA) template-generation approaches. Constrained ICA then used the templates to estimate subject-specific state patterns and continuous loadings in independent FBIRN schizophrenia and ADNI Alzheimer's disease cohorts. ICA loadings were calibrated by their contribution to reconstruction of the original feature matrix. Fractional occupancy and conditional mean dwell time were calculated from the state with the largest absolute calibrated loading at each observation. The predefined templates avoided the need for dataset-specific state discovery and post-hoc state matching. In both clinical cohorts, the analysis identified state-dependent, distributed edgewise differences and differences in selected temporal summaries. Nominal frequency-resolved findings varied across states and moment-frequency bins and were treated as exploratory. NeuroMark dFNC provides a common state space for cross-cohort comparison while retaining subject-specific connectivity patterns and continuous state expression.

papers.title: Neural categorisation of rhythm in human newborns
papers.abstract: Music is ubiquitous across cultures, and humans engage in social interactions through music from early in life. A cornerstone of these interactions is rhythm categorisation, allowing the sheer diversity of rhythmic inputs to be mapped onto internal rhythm categories. The pervasiveness of certain rhythm categories across cultures suggests that rhythm categorisation may be partially rooted in neurobiological predispositions constraining the internal representations of rhythm. However, this view appears to conflict with the diversity of music practices across cultures, which points to a role of experience in rhythm categorisation. To assess the relative contributions of neurobiological predispositions and experience, we tested 0- to 3-day-old newborns, capitalising on their minimal postnatal experience with music. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we recorded, in newborns and adults, brain responses to drum sounds whose pattern of relative interval duration ranged from isochronous to long-short rhythms (1:1 - 2:1 interval ratio). Results indicate significant categorisation in newborns's neural responses, with a representational structure that correlate with those of adults, yet with a greater degree of differentiation across rhythms. These findings reveal neurobiological predispositions enabling rhythm categorisation to be present at birth and further shaped across the lifespan, highlighting the evolutionary roots and plasticity supporting this human cultural practice.

papers.title: Brain-thought states during movie-watching reflect shared sensory anchors and film- and person- specific processes in association cortex
papers.abstract: Naturalistic paradigms such as movie-watching have transformed functional neuroimaging by capturing cognitive dynamics during rich, real-world experiences. A fundamental challenge, however, is determining whether the neural signatures identified during these experiences reflect general principles of cognition or the specific contexts in which they are measured. To address this question, we combined fMRI data from participants watching eight diverse films with continuous reports of ongoing thought. We found that the generalizability of brain-thought relationships depends on the cognitive process being recruited. Neural signatures linked to sensory processing remained robust across films, whereas those involving memory-related association networks depended on how we modelled between-film variability, indicating that cognition becomes increasingly context-dependent along the cortical hierarchy from sensory to association cortex. Within default and limbic networks, we identified two contrasting memory-related states with opposite consequences for comprehension. One, reflecting the integration of prior knowledge with ongoing experience, predicted better narrative comprehension and was revealed only after accounting for between-film variability. The other, associated with stimulus-independent thought, predicted poorer comprehension and emerged only when between-film variability was not modelled. Together, these findings establish when brain-experience relationships measured during naturalistic paradigms can generalize across contexts and when they instead reflect interactions between cognition and the specific environments in which cognition unfolds. More broadly, the consistency of a given brain-experiential association may depend less on where it occurs in the brain and more on the viewer's contextual experience: perceiving the film, drawing on memory to understand it, or drifting away.

papers.title: Brainstem cholinergic cell loss causes slowly-developing motor impairments
papers.abstract: Pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) cholinergic degeneration is a feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is difficult to isolate the symptoms and circuit alterations caused by cholinergic cell loss in PD, where multiple nuclei are simultaneously degenerating. Here we develop a novel mouse model of brainstem cholinergic cell loss to define the timeline of symptom development and map physiological adaptations within the brainstem. Mild motor symptoms, including balance and motor learning deficits reminiscent of early-stage PD, developed after cholinergic lesion with an unexpected long delay. Ex vivo whole-cell recordings showed that cholinergic cell loss increased excitatory synaptic drive onto glutamatergic PPN neurons and increased their intrinsic ability to generate sustained action potential output. In parallel, fiber photometry experiments revealed a slight increase in glutamatergic sensory responsiveness that closely tracked the delayed onset of behavioral symptoms. Together, these results reveal that brainstem cholinergic cell loss triggers the reorganization of motor-related brainstem circuits, providing critical insight into the consequences of non-dopaminergic degeneration in PD.

papers.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
papers.abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group x task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group x task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

papers.title: Source-Decomposed Multimodal Graph Connectivity: A Temporal Mixture-Manifold Pipeline for Tracking Ischemic Injury and Treatment
papers.abstract: To capture the complex, dynamic network reorganization following acute focal brain injuries that standard static or unimodal neuroimaging frameworks routinely miss, we present an open, reproducible computational multimodal pipeline that integrates resting state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) into dynamic, source-decomposed graph networks. This framework preserves sub-voxel, multi-peak distributional dynamics over time by modeling regional blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals within sliding windows using a Gaussian mixture model, with model complexity dynamically optimized. The resulting pairwise similarities define time-varying edge weights across local, nonlocal, and DTI-supported structural sources, unifying them into a multimodal connectivity manifold that precisely quantifies node strength, topological turnover, and boundary modifications. Applied to a non-human primate model of photothrombotic ischemia, the methodology revealed severe post-injury disruptions, with 66 of 144 nodes (45.8%) fundamentally altering their connectivity across localized sources. Furthermore, coupling this architecture with an Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) allowed for the continuous tracking of a tissue reversibility coordinate, yielding earlier detection of metabolic state collapse than uni-modal baselines and generating a forecast-divergence index as a rigorous early-warning signal. Extended across post-injury treatment boundaries to evaluate network recovery toward baseline, this interpretable, modality-aware framework establishes a standardized, shareable methodological foundation for tracking complex pathophysiological dynamics in neuroinformatics research.

papers.title: History of opioid use disorder correlates with altered neuroimmune signatures in the human dorsal root ganglia
papers.abstract: Understanding mechanisms for the negative reinforcing effects of opioids are fundamental to improving patient care. Using human dorsal root ganglia (DRG) from donors with and without opioid use disorder (OUD), we set out to examine functional and molecular correlates of chronic opioid use. At a molecular level, we detected disrupted immune signatures throughout cells in the peripheral nervous system (PNS), spanning glial-neuroimmune interactions to changes in non-neuronal senescence. At the physiological level these changes are paired with sensitization of DRG sensory neurons. Our findings reveal a neuro-inflammatory state in the PNS of individuals with OUD. Targeting therapeutics towards these PNS-based mechanisms could be an approach to alleviating the negative reinforcing effects of opioids.

papers.title: Striatal D2-neurons gate D1-mediated associative encoding under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Goal-directed actions are established through the encoding of predictive relationships between behaviour and its consequences, a process involving dopamine-dependent plasticity in the dorsal striatum. Early phases of learning entail complex associative landscapes from which useful action-outcome contingencies must be identified. Although dopamine processes are central to associative learning, the cellular mechanisms through which behaviourally relevant plasticity is selected from competing signalling events remain unknown. Here we show that D2-spiny projection neurons (D2-SPNs) are transiently recruited during the earliest stages of instrumental learning, when critical action-outcome contingencies emerge. We identify a dominant cell-to-cell transmodulation process by which D2-SPNs regulate dopamine-dependent signalling by constraining protein kinase A activity in D1-SPNs. This mechanism overrides extracellular dopamine signals and can be reproduced in vivo through calibrated optogenetic activation of cAMP signalling. Enhancing D2[->]D1-SPN transmodulation during uncertain reinforcement schedules durably improves action-outcome encoding, revealing a mechanism through which striatal networks promote relevant contingencies under associative ambiguity.

papers.title: Neuronal avalanches in awake macaque V1 and V4
papers.abstract: Neuronal avalanches are cascades of synchronised activity whose sizes follow power law. Analyses of avalanches shed light on cortical dynamics operating near a critical point. In awake monkeys, avalanches were found in motor and premotor cortex, where they are invariant to temporal binning, detection threshold and the number of electrodes employed. Whether awake primate early visual cortex, which receives strong structured afferent drive, shares these properties has not been tested. We analyzed a public 1,024-channel resting-state dataset from V1 and V4 of two macaques. In both animals avalanche sizes followed power laws over more than 10-fold range, the exponent scaled with bin width as alpha proportional to delta-t to the power beta (beta = -0.045 and -0.031), and the distributions ended at a cutoff proportional to the number of electrodes analysed. Raising the detection threshold from 1.5 to 4.5 standard deviations (SDs) removed over 99% of events but changed alpha by only 0.02-0.05 per SD, whereas randomly removing the same events destroyed the power law. Per-electrode shuffling abolished all heavy tails. Eye closure shifted alpha, beta and the branching ratio by less than predefined equivalence bounds, far below the reproducible differences between recording sites. Avalanche organisation therefore extends to awake early visual cortex.
